solution:
The ray falls on the face AB at right angles, so it enters the prism WITHOUT bending: at normal incidence both the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction are zero. It therefore travels straight across the prism and meets the second face AC.
The geometry fixes the angle of incidence there. The ray inside the prism is perpendicular to AB, and the prism is equilateral so that each of its angles is \(60^{\circ}\); the normal to AC therefore makes an angle of \(60^{\circ}\) with the ray. Hence the ray strikes AC at an angle of incidence
\(i = 60^{\circ}\).
Now compare this with the critical angle. The passage gives \(i_c = 24{\cdot}5^{\circ}\) for strontium titanate, and
\(60^{\circ} > 24{\cdot}5^{\circ}\),
so the light cannot pass out through AC. It undergoes TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION at that face, the angle of reflection being \(60^{\circ}\) as well.
The reflected ray then travels down through the prism and meets the third face BC along ITS normal, so it emerges through BC without any further bending.
Path to be traced, therefore: in through AB undeviated, total internal reflection at AC, and out through BC perpendicular to it, the ray having been turned through \(60^{\circ}\) altogether (\(180^{\circ} - 2 \times 60^{\circ}\) at the reflection).
note: Total internal reflection at i = 60 deg turns the ray through 180 - 120 = 60 deg, not 90.

solution:
**The answer is (C): 160 cm.**

**Two steps: find the focal length, then use the magnification condition.**

**Step 1: the focal length.** For a plano-convex lens, one surface has radius \(R\) and the other is flat \(\left(R \to \infty\right)\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(n-1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right) = \dfrac{n-1}{R}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 - 1}{40} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{40} = \dfrac{1}{80}\)

\(f = 80\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**Step 2: where the image is the same size as the object.** For a converging lens, \(\left|m\right| = 1\) with a **real** image occurs at one place only:

\(u = 2f\)

\(\boxed{\ \text{object distance} = 2 \times 80 = 160\ \mathrm{cm}\ }\)

*Confirming with the lens equation:* with \(u = -160\) and \(f = +80\),

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{80} + \dfrac{1}{-160} = \dfrac{2-1}{160} = \dfrac{1}{160}\)

so \(v = +160\) cm and \(m = v/u = 160/\left(-160\right) = -1\), same size, **inverted**, real \(\checkmark\).

**Option (B), 80 cm, is the focal length itself**, and it is the trap: an object at \(f\) produces an image at **infinity**, not one of equal size. Stopping after step 1 lands exactly on it.

**Why \(2f\) is the unique real-image solution.** Writing \(m = f/\left(f - u_{\text{signed}}\right)\), the magnitude is \(1\) only when the object is at \(2f\) (image real and inverted) or at the lens itself (trivial). **A virtual image of a converging lens is always magnified**, never the same size, so no second answer exists on that side.

**\(u = v = 2f\) is a symmetric configuration**, and it is the minimum possible object-to-image distance for a real image with a converging lens, \(4f = 320\) cm here. Any other real-image arrangement puts them further apart. That fact is the basis of the **displacement method** for measuring focal length, in which the lens is moved between two positions that both give sharp images.

**A note on which face is curved.** The answer does not depend on it. Turning the lens round swaps a plane surface for a curved one and vice versa, and the lensmaker's formula gives the same \(f\) either way, a general property of thin lenses. Only the aberrations differ.

**The sign convention, briefly.** Distances are measured from the optical centre with light travelling left to right; the object distance is negative and a real image distance positive. Working with magnitudes and quoting the final answer as a distance, as above, avoids most sign errors, provided the lens equation itself is applied with signs intact.
note: For a lens m = v/u; the line used the mirror form with an extra factor of -1.

solution:
**Note:** As printed (NCERT Ex. 9.22), the focal length is 9 cm, the same as the card's distance, so the image would form at infinity and part (a) has no finite answer. Earlier NCERT editions give the focal length as 10 cm, and the working below uses 10 cm.

The card is at \(u = -9\,\text{cm}\) from a converging lens of focal length \(f = 10\,\text{cm}\), viewed with the eye close to the lens; the near point is \(D = 25\,\text{cm}\).

(a) Lens equation:

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{9 - 10}{90} = -\dfrac{1}{90}\)

\(v = -90\,\text{cm}\), a virtual image on the same side as the card.

\(|m| = \left|\dfrac{v}{u}\right| = \dfrac{90}{9} = 10\)

Area scales as the SQUARE of the linear magnification, so each square becomes

\(10 \times 10 \times 1 = 100\,\text{mm}^{2} = 1\,\text{cm}^{2}\)

(b) Angular magnification of a simple magnifier used this way is set by how much closer than the near point the object can be brought:

\(\text{MP} = \dfrac{D}{|u|} = \dfrac{25}{9} = 2.8\)

(c) NO: they are different quantities and they happen to differ here. Linear magnification \(|v/u|\) compares the physical SIZE of image and object. Angular magnification compares the angle the image subtends at the eye with the angle the object would subtend if placed at the near point, and equals \(D/|u|\). They coincide only when the image itself is formed at the near point, i.e. \(|v| = 25\,\text{cm}\); here \(|v| = 90\,\text{cm}\), so \(10 \ne 2.8\).

(a) \(|m| = 10\); each square has area \(100\,\text{mm}^{2} = 1\,\text{cm}^{2}\) in the virtual image.
(b) Magnifying power \(= 2.8\).
(c) No: the two are equal only when the image is at the near point.

Each square is \(1\,\text{mm}^{2}\) and its virtual image is to be \(6.25\,\text{mm}^{2}\). Area goes as the square of the linear magnification, so

\(|m| = \sqrt{\dfrac{6.25}{1}} = 2.5\)

The image is virtual and erect, on the same side as the object, so \(v = 2.5u\). With \(f = 10\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2.5u} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{10}\)

\(\dfrac{1 - 2.5}{2.5u} = \dfrac{1}{10} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{-1.5}{2.5u} = \dfrac{1}{10} \quad\Rightarrow\quad u = -6\,\text{cm}\)

\(|v| = 2.5 \times 6 = 15\,\text{cm}\)

The image lies only \(15\,\text{cm}\) from the eye, which is CLOSER than the near point of \(25\,\text{cm}\). A normal eye cannot focus that close, so although the squares are magnified they will not be seen distinctly.

The object must be \(6\,\text{cm}\) from the magnifying glass. No: the virtual image forms at \(15\,\text{cm}\), inside the near point, so the squares cannot be seen distinctly with the eye close to the magnifier.

The lens of Exercise 9.22 has \(f = 10\,\text{cm}\); the near point is \(D = 25\,\text{cm}\).

(a) A simple magnifier gives its greatest angular magnification when the eye is working hardest, i.e. when the virtual image is formed right at the near point, \(v = -25\,\text{cm}\).

\(\dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{f} = -\dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{1}{10} = -0.14\)

\(u = -7.14\,\text{cm}\)

So the lens is held \(7.14\,\text{cm}\) from the card sheet.

(b) \(|m| = \left|\dfrac{v}{u}\right| = \dfrac{25}{7.14} = 3.5\)

(c) Magnifying power \(= \dfrac{D}{|u|} = \dfrac{25}{7.14} = 3.5\), equivalently \(1 + \dfrac{D}{f} = 1 + 2.5 = 3.5\).

YES, they are equal in this case, and for the reason identified in Exercise 9.22: the two quantities agree exactly when the image is formed at the near point, which is the condition imposed in part (a).

(a) The lens should be held \(7.14\,\text{cm}\) from the sheet.
(b) Magnification \(= 3.5\).
(c) Magnifying power \(= 3.5\), yes, equal, because the image is at the near point.

solution:
**Refraction at a SINGLE spherical surface**, not a lens, so the formula is

\(\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\)

**Sign convention.** Light travels left to right; the object is on the left, so \(u = -6\) cm. The surface is convex towards the incoming light, so \(R = +24\) cm. And \(n_1 = 1\) (air), \(n_2 = 1{\cdot}5\) (glass).

**Substituting:**

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} - \dfrac{1{\cdot}0}{-6} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 - 1{\cdot}0}{24}\)

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{24} = \dfrac{1}{48}\)

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} = \dfrac{1}{48} - \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1 - 8}{48} = -\dfrac{7}{48}\)

\(v = 1{\cdot}5\times\left(-\dfrac{48}{7}\right) = -\dfrac{72}{7}\)

\(\boxed{\ v = -10{\cdot}29\ \mathrm{cm} \quad\text{: the image is VIRTUAL}\ }\)

**It lies about \(10{\cdot}3\) cm from the surface, on the SAME SIDE as the object**, that is, in the air, \(10{\cdot}3\) cm in front of the surface. It is virtual, erect, and magnified.

**The negative sign is the whole of "nature".** A positive \(v\) would place the image inside the glass, where the refracted light actually travels, and it would be **real**. A negative \(v\) means the refracted rays still **diverge** after the surface, and only their backward extensions meet.

**Why it had to be virtual, without any arithmetic.** This surface's first focal length is

\(f_1 = \dfrac{n_1R}{n_2 - n_1} = \dfrac{24}{0{\cdot}5} = 48\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**and a real image requires the object to lie OUTSIDE it.** At \(6\) cm the object is far inside \(48\) cm, so the image could only be virtual, a check worth making before the substitution rather than after.

**\(6\) cm is very close indeed**, an eighth of the first focal length. The surface bends the rays towards the axis, but nowhere near enough to make them converge; it merely makes them diverge less steeply, which the eye reads as an enlarged image further away.

**Two errors this problem invites.** Using the thin-lens formula \(1/v - 1/u = 1/f\) treats two surfaces where there is one, and gives a different answer. And taking \(R = -24\) reverses the surface's curvature: **convex towards the incoming light means \(R\) is positive**, since the centre of curvature lies on the outgoing side.

**The magnification**, for completeness:

\(m = \dfrac{n_1v}{n_2u} = \dfrac{\left(1\right)\left(-10{\cdot}29\right)}{\left(1{\cdot}5\right)\left(-6\right)} = +1{\cdot}14\)

**erect and slightly enlarged**, consistent with a virtual image. *(Note this is not \(v/u\); a refracting surface with different media on its two sides carries the index ratio as well.)*

**The prism is an isosceles right-angled triangle** with the right angle at \(B\), and therefore \(45^\circ\) at both \(A\) and \(C\). The ray \(MN\) arrives **normally** on face \(AB\).

**What happens at the first face.** Incidence is normal, so the ray enters **without bending** and travels straight on inside the glass towards the hypotenuse \(AC\).

**The angle at the hypotenuse.** \(AC\) is inclined at \(45^\circ\), so the ray, still horizontal, meets it at

\(i = 45^\circ\ \text{to the normal of } AC\)

**That \(45^\circ\) is fixed by the geometry and is the same in both parts.** Only the critical angle changes, and everything turns on how it compares.

**(i) Refractive index \(\sqrt{2}\).**

\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad i_c = 45^\circ\)

**The angle of incidence EQUALS the critical angle exactly.**

\(\boxed{\ i = i_c \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{the ray GRAZES along the surface } AC\ }\)

*To trace it:* the ray enters normally at \(N\), runs horizontally to \(AC\), and there emerges **at \(90^\circ\) to the normal**, that is, travelling **along the face \(AC\) itself**, sliding down the hypotenuse rather than leaving into the air or turning back into the glass. This is the threshold case, and it belongs to neither refraction nor total reflection properly.

**(ii) Refractive index \(\sqrt{3}\).**

\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 0{\cdot}577 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad i_c = 35{\cdot}3^\circ < 45^\circ\)

**The angle of incidence now EXCEEDS the critical angle.**

\(\boxed{\ i > i_c \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION at } AC\ }\)

*To trace it:* the ray enters normally at \(N\), runs horizontally to \(AC\), and is **totally reflected there** through \(90^\circ\). It then travels **vertically downwards**, strikes the base \(BC\) **normally**, and emerges from \(BC\) **without bending**, continuing straight down.

**The ray has been turned through exactly \(90^\circ\)** by a single reflection, and this is precisely how a right-angled prism is used in periscopes and binoculars.

**Why a prism rather than a mirror.** Total internal reflection is **total**, essentially no light is lost, where a silvered mirror reflects perhaps \(90\%\) and tarnishes with age. The prism needs no coating at all; the reflection is a property of the glass-air boundary.

**The single principle behind both parts.** The geometry fixes \(i = 45^\circ\); the material fixes \(i_c\); and comparing the two decides the outcome. **A higher refractive index means a smaller critical angle and therefore easier total internal reflection**, which is why \(\sqrt{3}\) reflects where \(\sqrt{2}\) only just fails to.

**Finding the angle of the prism.**

At minimum deviation the prism formula is

\(\mu = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}\)

The condition given is \(\delta_m = A\), so the numerator becomes \(\sin A\):

\(\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + A}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{\sin A}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}\)

Use the double-angle identity \(\sin A = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)\). The sine cancels, which is the whole trick of this question:

\(\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{2\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)} = 2\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)\)

\(\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{A}{2} = 30^\circ\)

\(A = 60^\circ\)

This is the familiar equilateral prism, and with \(\delta_m = A = 60^\circ\) the ray enters at \(i = (A + \delta_m)/2 = 60^\circ\), a neat special case where the angle of incidence, the prism angle and the minimum deviation are all equal.

**The effect of immersing the prism in water.**

Only the **relative** refractive index enters the prism formula, so what matters is the index of the glass *with respect to its surroundings*:

\(^{w}\mu_g = \dfrac{\mu_g}{\mu_w} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}732}{1{\cdot}33} \approx 1{\cdot}30\)

This is smaller than \(1{\cdot}732\), and since \(\delta_m\) increases with the relative index for a fixed \(A\), **the angle of minimum deviation decreases.**

Putting a number to it, with \(A\) still \(60^\circ\):

\(\sin\left(\dfrac{60^\circ + \delta_m'}{2}\right) = 1{\cdot}30 \times \sin 30^\circ = 0{\cdot}650\)

\(\dfrac{60^\circ + \delta_m'}{2} \approx 40{\cdot}5^\circ \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \delta_m' \approx 21^\circ\)

So the deviation falls from \(60^\circ\) to about \(21^\circ\), a large change, because water removes most of the contrast in optical density that made the glass bend light in the first place.

The limiting case makes the reasoning obvious: were the prism immersed in a liquid of index exactly \(\sqrt{3}\), the relative index would be 1, there would be no refraction at either face, and the deviation would be zero. The prism would simply vanish from view.

At minimum deviation the prism formula is

\(n = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + D_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}\)

With \(A = 60^\circ\) and \(D_m = 40^\circ\):

\(n = \dfrac{\sin 50^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = \dfrac{0.766}{0.5} = 1.53\)

When the prism is immersed in water the RELATIVE refractive index of glass with respect to water is what enters the formula:

\(n_{gw} = \dfrac{1.53}{1.33} = 1.150\)

\(\sin\left(\dfrac{60^\circ + D_m'}{2}\right) = n_{gw}\sin 30^\circ = 1.150 \times 0.5 = 0.575\)

\(\dfrac{60^\circ + D_m'}{2} = \sin^{-1}(0.575) = 35.1^\circ\)

\(D_m' = 70.2^\circ - 60^\circ = 10.2^\circ\)

Refractive index of the prism \(= 1.53\); the new angle of minimum deviation in water is about \(10^\circ\).
